overview: EBS (Elastic Block Store) is a network-attached block drive for EC2 that persists data independently of instance lifetime, but is locked to a single Availability Zone and mounted to one instance at a time. The exam tests the consequences of those constraints: how you bill provisioned size and IOPS, why a snapshot is the only path to move or copy a volume across AZs or Regions, and what happens to volumes when an instance terminates. On top of snapshots sit three features — Archive (cheap, slow restore), Recycle Bin (recover deleted snapshots for 1 day to 1 year) and Fast Snapshot Restore (remove first-use latency for a price) — that are classic cost-vs-latency and recovery scenarios.

coreConcepts.definition: A network drive (not a physical drive) that you attach to an EC2 instance while it runs, letting the instance persist data even after termination; often described as a "network USB stick".
Because EBS communicates with the instance over the network, there may be a bit of latency compared with instance storage.
An EBS volume can be detached from one EC2 instance and attached to another quickly; at the CCP level it can only be mounted to one instance at a time.
An EBS volume is locked to a specific Availability Zone — a volume in us-east-1a cannot be attached to an instance in us-east-1b; moving across AZs requires a snapshot.
A volume has provisioned capacity (size in GB and IOPS) that you choose up front; capacity can be increased over time.
You are billed for all the provisioned capacity, regardless of how much of it the instance actually uses.
A point-in-time backup of an EBS volume; detaching the volume first is not necessary but is recommended.

coreConcepts.term: Snapshot copy across AZ or Region
coreConcepts.definition: Snapshots can be copied across Availability Zones or Regions, and restoring a snapshot in another AZ creates a volume there — the standard way to move a volume.
An EBS attribute controlling what happens to the volume when the attached EC2 instance terminates; controllable via AWS console or AWS CLI.
By default the root EBS volume is deleted on instance termination (attribute enabled); by default any other attached EBS volume is not deleted (attribute disabled).
Moves a snapshot to an "archive tier" that is 75% cheaper, with restore taking within 24 to 72 hours.
Rules that retain deleted snapshots so you can recover them after an accidental deletion; retention is specified from 1 day to 1 year.
Forces full initialization of a snapshot so a restored volume has no latency on first use; costs extra ($$$).

mustRemember: An EBS volume is bound to exactly one Availability Zone; a us-east-1a volume cannot attach to us-east-1b.
To move a volume across AZs (or copy to another Region), snapshot it and restore/copy the snapshot.
You are billed for the full provisioned capacity (GBs and IOPS), not for the portion used.
Volume capacity can be increased over time; provisioned size/IOPS is a chosen quantity, not a ceiling on usage.
By default, the root EBS volume IS deleted when the instance terminates (Delete on Termination enabled).
By default, non-root attached EBS volumes are NOT deleted when the instance terminates (attribute disabled).
Delete on Termination can be changed via the AWS console or AWS CLI — e.g. to preserve the root volume.
Detaching a volume before snapshotting is not required, but is recommended.
EBS Snapshot Archive is 75% cheaper and restores within 24 to 72 hours.
Recycle Bin retention for deleted snapshots is from 1 day to 1 year.
Fast Snapshot Restore removes first-use latency by full initialization of the snapshot, and costs extra.

keyComparisons.difference: EBS is a network drive that persists independently of the instance; an instance store is tied to the physical host and does not survive the way a detachable network drive does.
Within one AZ a volume can be detached and re-attached quickly; across AZs you must snapshot and restore.

keyComparisons.items: Root volume vs non-root volume on termination
keyComparisons.difference: Root volume is deleted by default; additional data volumes are kept by default.

keyComparisons.items: EBS Snapshot vs EBS Snapshot Archive
keyComparisons.difference: Standard snapshots restore quickly; archive copies are 75% cheaper but take 24-72 hours to restore.

keyComparisons.items: EBS Snapshot Archive vs Recycle Bin
keyComparisons.difference: Archive is a cheap long-term storage tier for snapshots you keep; Recycle Bin retains snapshots you deleted so they can be recovered (1 day-1 year).

keyComparisons.items: Recycle Bin vs Fast Snapshot Restore
keyComparisons.difference: Recycle Bin answers "I deleted it by accident"; FSR answers "restore is too slow on first use" and is paid for with extra cost.

keyComparisons.items: Snapshot taken without detach vs after detach
keyComparisons.difference: Both are possible — detaching is optional but recommended for a clean point-in-time backup.
Billing follows provisioned GB and IOPS, so over-provisioning costs money even when idle.

commonMisunderstandings: An EBS volume can be attached to instances in any AZ in the Region — it cannot; it is locked to its AZ.
You only pay for the storage you fill up — you pay for all provisioned capacity, including provisioned IOPS.
All attached volumes are deleted when the instance terminates — only the root volume is deleted by default.
You must detach a volume before you can snapshot it — you need not, though it is recommended.
Snapshots are AZ-bound like volumes — snapshots can be copied across AZs and Regions.
Deleting a snapshot is always final — a Recycle Bin rule can retain deleted snapshots from 1 day to 1 year.
Archive tier is just cheaper snapshots with the same restore time — restore from archive takes 24 to 72 hours.
FSR makes the snapshot smaller or cheaper — FSR forces full initialization to remove first-use latency and costs extra.
mentalModels: Think of EBS as a "network USB stick": you plug it into an instance, unplug and move it — but only within the same AZ.
Think of the AZ as the building the drive is physically locked inside; to get it into another building you ship a copy (the snapshot).
Think of billing as renting a parking space by size and speed, not by how often you park.
Think of Delete on Termination as a checkbox on each volume: on for the root by default, off for the others.
Think of Snapshot Archive as the cold warehouse, Recycle Bin as the trash can with an undo window, and FSR as paying to pre-warm the engine.
edgeCases: A volume can be unattached entirely (shown as unattached alongside instances in different AZs) — an unattached volume still incurs provisioned-capacity billing.
Delete on Termination is per-volume, so you can run a non-root volume with it enabled or a root volume with it disabled.
Use case for disabling it on the root volume: preserve the root volume when the instance is terminated.
Archive restore time is a range (24 to 72 hours), not a fixed value, and cannot be shortened by FSR.
Recycle Bin must be set up with rules in advance — retention of 1 day to 1 year applies only to snapshots covered by a rule.
Snapshotting a live volume is allowed without detaching, so an exam option that makes detaching mandatory is wrong.
FSR costs extra ($$$), so it is a latency-requirement choice, not a cost-optimization choice.

whenToUse.situation: Data must survive the termination of the EC2 instance it is attached to
whenToUse.use: EBS volume instead of ephemeral instance storage

whenToUse.situation: A volume must be used by an instance in a different Availability Zone
whenToUse.use: Snapshot the volume and restore it as a new volume in the target AZ

whenToUse.situation: Copy a workload's volume to another Region
whenToUse.use: Copy the snapshot across the Region, then restore

whenToUse.situation: Keep the root volume after the instance is terminated
whenToUse.use: Disable the Delete on Termination attribute on the root volume

whenToUse.situation: Keep a rarely accessed backup at minimum cost and slow restore is acceptable
whenToUse.use: Move the snapshot to EBS Snapshot Archive (75% cheaper, restore in 24-72 hours)

whenToUse.situation: Protect against accidental deletion of snapshots for a defined period
whenToUse.use: Recycle Bin for EBS Snapshots with a retention of 1 day to 1 year

whenToUse.situation: Restored volumes must have no latency on first use
whenToUse.use: Enable Fast Snapshot Restore, accepting the extra cost

examTraps.trap: Pick a volume in another AZ and attach it directly.
examTraps.correction: A volume cannot cross AZs; snapshot it and restore in the target AZ.

examTraps.trap: Choose the smallest volume to save money.
examTraps.correction: Billing is on provisioned size and IOPS, so size/IOPS should match the requirement, not be minimized.

examTraps.trap: Assume all volumes are deleted at termination.
examTraps.correction: Only the root volume is deleted by default; other volumes persist (attribute disabled).

examTraps.trap: Say snapshotting requires the volume to be detached first.
examTraps.correction: Detaching is not necessary, only recommended.

examTraps.trap: Use Archive for a workload needing fast restore.
examTraps.correction: Archive restore takes 24 to 72 hours; use a standard snapshot (or FSR) when speed matters.

examTraps.trap: Use Fast Snapshot Restore to reduce snapshot storage cost.
examTraps.correction: FSR removes first-use latency and costs extra; use Archive for cost reduction.

examTraps.trap: Expect Recycle Bin to retain snapshots indefinitely.
examTraps.correction: Retention is set by rule and ranges from 1 day to 1 year.

examTraps.trap: Assume an unattached volume is free.
examTraps.correction: Provisioned capacity is billed whether or not the volume is attached.

beyondSource: (Tutor knowledge) The source says one instance at a time "at the CCP level"; on the SAA exam, multi-attach is a fact for specific EBS volume types (io1/io2) in the same AZ, and is still not a way to cross AZs.

(Tutor knowledge) EBS volume types (gp2/gp3, io1/io2, st1, sc1) are examinable under SAA "block storage options (HDD vs SSD)" and "selecting the appropriate storage tier"; the AZ lock and snapshot mechanics on this page apply to all of them.
